The user is developing a fictional world called Hiigarraa. The Thirene Empire and the other empires used magic extensively, and magic became more powerful over time as the moon Illune drew closer to Hiigarraa for a reason unknown to the people of that world.

In the user's mythology, Illune's approach was caused by Nothing and the Goddess of Darkness and Mercy fighting; Nothing was slowly winning and drawing closer to the center of The One Above All's creations. Nothing was imprisoned within Illune and briefly broke a small bond of that prison, reaching out and causing The Sundering.

The Thirene Empire fell during The Sundering, a magical cataclysm triggered when Illune came too close to Hiigarraa and Nothing briefly reached beyond its prison. The Sundering caused earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanoes, and other natural disasters across the world; Illune's proximity also made magic go wild.

The Eohagana Dynasty, Vrusitara Empire, Thirene Empire, and an as-yet-unnamed First Empire all regularly used magic, which was integrated into their societies. The user's account says magic grew increasingly potent as Illune approached Hiigarraa.

Hiigarraa has three other moons—Lune, Allune, and Ellune—and three legendary magical artifacts or key-devices tied to those moons. The artifacts were made during the world's creation and were discovered by one or more adventuring parties in different empire eras. Collecting the key-devices and activating Lune, Allune, and Ellune enabled a partial resealing of Illune, Nothing, and the Goddess of Mercy and Death; this prevented The Sundering from utterly destroying Hiigarraa.

On 2023-05-23, the user asked the assistant to remember general information from an online website about the differences between deeds and agreements in Australia. The information stated that both can record legally binding deals, but differ in their legal requirements and execution; businesses should understand the distinction when structuring transactions to manage litigation risk and resolve disputes.

The online information defined an agreement as an understanding or arrangement between two or more parties. For an agreement to be legally binding, it must have offer and acceptance, an intention to be legally bound, and consideration: a promise or obligation forming part of a bargain in which something of value is given in return, often a counter-promise.

The online information described a deed as a special type of promise or commitment indicating a particularly serious or solemn intention by the executing party to do what was promised. A deed can pass or confer legal or equitable interests in property or another right, create an obligation binding on a person, or affirm an agreement that passes such an interest or right.

The online information listed documents commonly executed as deeds: Deed Polls, Escrow Deeds, Confidentiality Deeds, Deeds of Termination, Settlement Deeds, Deeds of Company Arrangement, Forbearance Deeds, Guarantee Deeds, Novation Deeds, and Indemnity Deeds. It said parties commonly enter into a deed of settlement and release to resolve disputes, particularly litigation. It also stated that legislation requires certain documents to be executed as deeds; for example, in every Australian state and territory except the Australian Capital Territory, certain assurances of land, including conveyances and dispositions, must be made by deed.

The online information stated that, at common law, a deed must be written on parchment, vellum, or paper, have a personal seal placed on it, and be delivered to the other party. It said legislation across all Australian jurisdictions has modified these common-law requirements. Australian companies may execute a document as a deed if it is expressed to be “executed as a deed” and signed in accordance with the document-execution provisions of the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth).

The online information stated that in New South Wales, a deed signed by an individual must be signed and witnessed by someone who is not a party to the deed. The deed is deemed sealed if it is expressed to be a deed, meaning the document expressly states that it is executed as a deed.

The online information stated that deeds may be created in electronic form and signed and witnessed electronically in New South Wales, Victoria, and Queensland. It said electronic execution of deeds is not permitted in South Australia, Western Australia, the Northern Territory, Tasmania, or the Australian Capital Territory. It also said the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth) was recently amended to allow electronic execution of deeds, subject to certain conditions. Where a deed is executed by a mix of companies and individuals, the relevant provisions should be considered carefully because the law governing deed execution is not uniform.

The online information compared deeds and agreements as follows: a deed does not require consideration, unlike a valid agreement, and may overcome enforcement difficulties where no consideration is provided; a deed must be executed in writing, whereas an agreement can be oral or written unless statute specifies otherwise; and a deed generally has a longer limitation period for actions than an agreement.

The online information stated that the limitation period for breach of contract is six years in all Australian states and territories except the Northern Territory, where it is three years. For an action founded on a deed, it gave limitation periods of 15 years in Victoria and South Australia, and 12 years in New South Wales, the Australian Capital Territory, Queensland, Tasmania, Western Australia, and the Northern Territory, running from the date the cause of action arose.

The online information stated that equitable remedies are unavailable for actions founded on deeds that contain no consideration. It said deeds are generally not enforceable in equity without consideration, citing the maxim “equity will not support a volunteer.”
